newsitem.title: GERMANY: German health officials make new ruling on pill.
newsitem.headline: German health officials make new ruling on pill.

text.p: The German drug regulatory agency Bundesinstitut fuer Arzneimittel said on Tuesday it has agreed to keep an ongoing restriction on the use of certain contraceptive pills that may pose health risks.

German authorities said the ruling, which made permanent a temporary ban, was justified because there was no new data to disprove earlier reports that the so-called "third generation" birth control pills raises the chance of blood clots.

The decision marks the latest twist in a long-running dispute between drugs groups and health authorities that erupted in November 1995 when a British medical study said the pills doubled the chances for women to develop blood clots.
Third-generation pills are low-dosage contraceptive pills containing desogestrel or gestodene.

German drugs company Schering AG, the world's leading maker of oral contraceptives, on Tuesday again protested the ruling, saying the studies were not conclusive. Germany is currently the only European nation with restrictions on the these pills.

Physicians are now prohibited from prescribing these pills to women under 30 taking oral contraceptives for the first time. But the pills may be prescribed for older women as they are seen to lower the risk of heart attacks.

The ban also affected American Home Products Corp's Minulet and Tri-Minulet and Dutch firm Akzo Nobel NV's Marvellon and Mercilon brands and Schering's Femodene/Femovan, which is the group's seventh largest product.
Traders said the ruling helped knock Schering's share price nearly one percent lower to 138.90 marks at the close of bourse trading as the market worried about the ruling's impact on results.
But Schering said that the ruling would not impact results negatively as physicians would likely prescribe another pill made by Schering instead.
